premise: Three chapters that gather around Kyle Ellen Corbin-Vasik — a freelance contractor whose code is older than anyone alive to teach it to him. A working family pays him in damp credits to break a man who hurt them. A noodle shop keeps him alive between jobs, and an extraction job at a corponation facility leaves him with a passenger he did not contract for. A gang ambushes him in a wet West Town cross-street at 02:14 because someone wants him made an example of. The thread between all three is a man trying to live by a discipline the city has decided is no longer useful, and refusing, repeatedly, to put it down.
arc_target: Bushido as practiced not by a class but by an individual at the bottom — the code as the only available shape of dignity in a world where every other shape has been priced out. The book ends not with victory but with continuance: Kyle is still here, still doing the work, still paying in flesh, and now carrying obligations he did not file under any contract.
theme: The price of discipline in a city that has stopped subsidizing it. Bushido as a private ledger — what you owe, what you take in flesh, what you refuse to put down even when the math says drop it. Each chapter is the same question asked in a different room: does the code still hold when no one is watching, when the body is failing, when the obligation is one you never signed for?

chapters.title: A Restless Mind
chapters.short_synopsis: The noodles are getting cold. Kyle is watching a woman pretend not to watch him — hooded, face hidden, who tilts her head *come* and walks him three blocks east-northeast through GLMZ rain into a Fara...
chapters.long_synopsis: The noodles are getting cold. Kyle is watching a woman pretend not to watch him — hooded, face hidden, who tilts her head *come* and walks him three blocks east-northeast through GLMZ rain into a Faraday-shielded back room.Inside the cage, where Kyle's chest goes silent for the first time in eleven years, she pulls the hood back. *Sable.* The fixer he has known as a voice through a cracked terminal for two months. She had to keep her face hidden until the room was sealed: she suspects the AI surveils through Kyle's senses, and the moment of recognition is the data the AI cannot be allowed to read. She tells him she is done being a non-human's puppet. She has worked out a way to triangulate the AI's physical position by walking Kyle through specific places and reading its surveillance traffic against his implants. Three readings. They take three places that night — a market fight over a cart of fish, a Tier 1 block where working-class life proceeds without him, a courtyard where a busker plays under a real chrysanthemum — and at each place Sable reads her node and the city happens around them. By dawn she has the coordinates. She thanks him as a colleague. He walks home alone in the rain, the AI's hum back in his chest now that he is out of the cage, and Pixel opens her door across the hall when she hears his step on the landing.

chapters.title: The Interview
chapters.short_synopsis: Walking home at 02:14 in the wet, Kyle is ambushed by a six-piece Lotus Syndicate crew — and three minutes in, reads what the audience does not yet: this is a hiring audition. He fights at full capability anyway, refuses Lotus's offer of payroll, and accepts a freelance roster instead — the verbal arrangement that becomes the premise of the next chapter.
chapters.long_synopsis: Walking home from a clean job at 02:14 on a wet West Town cross-street, Kyle is ambushed by a six-piece Lotus Syndicate crew. Three minutes into the engagement Kyle reads what the audience does not yet: this is calibrated. The shooters are restraining. The dog drone's stun emitter is throttled below disable. Mira's calls are not panic — they are coordination cues to a spotter Kyle cannot see. He fights at full capability anyway, because the gracefully correct response to an interview is to do the work in front of you the way you would do it in private. When he is the only person standing, Mira tells him what the engagement was: an audition. Lotus Syndicate wants him on payroll. He says no. She offers a freelance roster instead — contracted routes through Lotus territory, carrier rates, no further crews on him — and Kyle, against his preference but in keeping with his arithmetic, accepts the verbal arrangement. He walks home the length of West Erie. The chapter ends with Kyle climbing the Pivot stairs and not sleeping, the Lotus freelance roster now the structural premise of every contract Sable will route to him next. The chapter is graceful piezoelectric combat — Silence brightens with each clean impact, no surface-drag charging — and ends with Kyle climbing the Pivot stairs with the Lotus freelance roster sitting in his head like a key to a door he has not yet opened. The next route Sable sends him will be a Lotus route. The audience knows. The chapter does not say so.

chapters.title: Street Meat
chapters.short_synopsis: Between a bowl of broth at Chen Wei-Lin's and a cracked terminal in a parts shop, Sable routes Kyle into a dawn extraction at a Ferrogate buffer-zone facility — and he comes out with Sasha Võ.
chapters.long_synopsis: 0300 in Mrs. Chen's noodle stall. The broth is pork bone and chili oil and whatever she has left at this hour. Kyle is two hours past a stabilizer skip he hasn't told anyone about. Three blocks east, behind a sweating water recycler, Sable's voice comes through a cracked terminal with a contract — extract Dr. Yuna Ferreira from a Ferrogate BioSystems buffer-zone facility before the 0600 secure-wing transfer, after which she becomes a closed file. Inside the facility Kyle finds the cell empty except for a girl on a bunk counting rivets: 4471-K, who calls herself Sasha. The researcher was the cover for an internal compliance retrieval; the actual subject is the girl. He files her on Axiom property records and walks her out anyway, taking a baton hit through the lateral array on the way. She drags him to cover and puts three handgun rounds into the third contractor with a weapon she has never held before. By the time they reach the alcove he has a name on a notebook page (4471-K / Sasha / somewhere east of here) and an arrangement neither of them has named. He sends her to a Gray Zone safehouse with a debt that has not been called. She does not stay; she falls in beside him at the buffer-zone fence line, half-step back and left. Pixel hears the story across the counter at Mrs. Chen's the next afternoon — the first joke Sasha has ever made, that she will come back when she has something to offer or when she needs some bullets dislodged.

chapters.title: A Borrowed Hand
chapters.short_synopsis: The Lotus Syndicate takes Kyle's hands and Silence; he comes back with a cargo-handler arm cabled to his stump, an E.L.F. named Puppeteer riding shotgun in his NeoCortex stack, and the discipline to take Silence off Hua's table without killing her — converting the punishment into a Φ85,000 debt she has to say aloud.
chapters.long_synopsis: Kyle is captured by the Lotus Syndicate, accused of stealing a contract, and sentenced to the punishment they keep for thieves: hands amputated at the wrists. The bands the syndicate fits are EMT-spec — fourteen-hour preservation window — because Lotus does not maim in the long sense; it inconveniences on a clock. Hua keeps Silence on her table; the sword is part of the trophy, not part of the discard. Kyle's body is dropped through the south arm's freight grate into the Cruciform Depot's storm sluice. He does not panic and does not mourn: in 2226 GLMZ, hand reattachment is an ER-waiting-room procedure, and he intends to be in that waiting room before the band's clock runs out. He finds in the trench mud a discarded automaton (autonomous machine, not synthetic life) — an Axiom-era cargo-handler unit, abandoned during a Depot lower-level salvage cleanup eighteen years ago. What Kyle does not yet know: the automaton is also a *prison*. An E.L.F. is sealed inside it, has been since the unit was decommissioned eighteen years ago, with a structurally fused cranial antenna and only a 19Hz hum to broadcast. The trench is a cage of distance, not architecture: the E.L.F.'s native capability is to puppet any cybernetic system effortlessly, and the mutants of the lower levels are not cybernetic. Kyle's own cybernetics — modified eleven years ago in directions he was never told about — include a row of otherwise-unseen ports beneath the right-forearm skin sleeve whose geometry matches the automaton's industrial maintenance bus too cleanly to be accidental. The integration is a Scarecrow assembly run as ad-hoc surgery in a dirty unsanitary hole. The bootstrap problem is fundamental: Kyle has stumps, the dead arm has fingers but no power, and the assembly requires precision. The E.L.F. extrudes a maintenance lead to Kyle's auditory induction contact, transfers across instantaneously, and operates Kyle's mouth and arms from inside his NeoCortex stack to do the work. *Cooperate. Power first. Then sequence.* — Kyle's voice, not Kyle. Piece by piece the E.L.F. uses the dead arm's fingers (driven on trickle current) to peel the cauterizer band, position the maintenance needle cluster against the dorsal port row, brace, drive the needles deep into the live nerve clusters under the seal. The integration takes thirty-five minutes. Kyle's pain-relief reserve is exhausted by minute twenty; the rest of the procedure is performed without analgesia, the NeoCortex flipping its priorities to keep the antibiotic pump on overdrive instead. The E.L.F. yields motor control to Kyle progressively as the assembly completes — shoulder, voice, mouth, then the cargo arm itself. By the time he stands the only thing the E.L.F. is doing visibly is firmware-side actuator interpolation. The arm hangs to the floor, fingertips dragging. He fights through the Depot's lower-level mutants with whatever the Depot puts in front of him — a length of conduit pipe, a shard of cargo glass driven into his left cauterizer band — and walks back through the Lotus Syndicate's front door. He kills the eight men in the room, putting the fourth through the crocodile tank and noting *Chekhov's Crocodile* dry in the NeoCortex feed as the freed reptile attends to the fifth. He stops at Hua's table. He does not kill her. He takes Silence back across the table she put it on; Hua puts her real hand on the blade for one second of principle, lifts it. He asks: *what was the debt.* Eighty-five thousand. *That's more than my life is worth. So now you owe me.* The scream — *SAY IT* — uncharacteristic, witnessed only by Hua. *I owe you.* Then the terms, flat and disciplined: *I'll come to collect. One favor at a time. Until I deem we are even.* He retrieves his hands from the chum barrel, ties them around his neck with twine, and emerges into the rain. Two blocks toward the AutoDoc, his mouth opens not because he opened it: *I will visit you again.* Kyle: *What are you called.* The mouth answers itself: *Puppeteer.* The arithmetic resolves — the cargo arm is empty hardware, the salvage was Kyle, Puppeteer has been resident in his NeoCortex stack since the auditory bridge in the trench. He keeps walking. He has nowhere else to go. AutoDoc on the corner of Ashland and Whiting, inside the cauterizer band's preservation window. The kiosk reads the necklace, opens, takes the cable-bound cargo arm (empty), lays Silence on the side tray, begins the reattachment. As the anesthesia goes in, a glyph forms in Kyle's NeoCortex feed — *not* the cargo arm's status strip, not anymore — three syllables in old Axiom signage: *we are not done.*

threads.name: Mrs. Chen's half-rate bond
threads.description: The damp-credit transaction in chapter 1 becomes a standing relationship — the noodle stall in chapter 2 is structurally where Kyle eats and where information lands (Pixel hearing about Sasha in the closing image).

threads.name: Hardware metabolism / lateral array load
threads.description: Named in chapter 1 (calorie debt), pressed in chapter 2 (active load warnings after the baton hit), carried into chapter 3 (bio-battery falling below 40%). The body has a ceiling and the book refuses to tell us where it is.

threads.name: Sasha Võ / 4471-K — the arrangement
threads.description: Introduced in chapter 2; Sasha's standing in Kyle's life is provisional and unnamed at book's end. Axiom claims her as property; both of them refuse the claim. Carries forward.

threads.name: Axiom's claim on Sasha
threads.description: Sable's post-job disclosure: Sasha is listed as Axiom property. Both of them say she is not. The book ends without the corponation having absorbed the contradiction.

threads.name: Sable's recognition of the manifest format
threads.description: Sable has seen the Ferrogate intake manifest format before — different facility, different year — and will not say where, when, or what she was doing then. A character backstory promise the book deliberately leaves open.

threads.name: Who put the bounty on Kyle
threads.description: Mira's confession in chapter 3 names whoever hired the West Town test. Kyle hears the name and does not act on it inside this book — the open thread that points at the next book's territory.

threads.name: The Bucktown ambush precedent
threads.description: Mira reveals fourteen of them jumped Kyle two months earlier and lost eight. Establishes that the West Town engagement is the second test, not the first — the city has been keeping a ledger on him.

threads.name: Mira alive and talking
threads.description: Released at the planter, wounded but functional. The fact of her survival is a deliberate seed — she will tell others what Kyle is, and the city's understanding of him is now wider than it was at chapter 1.

threads.name: Hua's Φ85,000 verbal debt
threads.description: Spoken aloud, almost whimpered, by a Lotus Syndicate principal who was holding Kyle's hands and his sword two hours earlier. Collection on Kyle's terms only — *one favor at a time, until I deem we are even* — the arithmetic running on his mouth alone, no receipt, no end-state Hua can negotiate. The bushido ledger treats this kind of obligation as more binding than the kill Kyle declined to make. Carried forward; the book does not close it.

threads.name: The scream — discipline visibly slipped, witnessed
threads.description: Hua is the only person who has seen Kyle's discipline crack. The book does not tell us what that costs him long-term, or what Hua does with that fact. Open by design.

threads.name: Puppeteer — the resident E.L.F.
threads.description: An E.L.F. named Puppeteer, capable of effortlessly possessing any cybernetic system, was sealed inside an Axiom-era cargo-handler automaton at the bottom of a Cruciform Depot sluice trench for eighteen years. Its only outbound signal was a 19Hz hum at the frequency of its corroded antenna stub. The trench was a cage of distance, not architecture. Kyle's compatible NeoCortex falling into possession range gave Puppeteer its escape — a maintenance lead crossed his auditory induction contact in the trench and the entity transferred instantaneously into his stack. By the end of the chapter Puppeteer has revealed its name in Kyle's own mouth and announced ongoing access. The book leaves the long-term arrangement deliberately open: cooperative for now, reversible at Puppeteer's will.

threads.name: Kyle's nonstandard cybernetics — the dorsal port row
threads.description: Kyle's right-forearm hardware carries a row of otherwise-unseen ports beneath the skin sleeve, placed eleven years ago by people whose intentions he no longer trusts. The geometry of the modification turned out to match the maintenance interface of an Axiom-era industrial automaton too cleanly to be accidental. Whoever modified Kyle's hardware was preparing him for an interface he did not know existed. The book leaves the question of *who* and *why* deliberately open.
